                    ### Question
                    A 38-year-old man presents with pruritus and jaundice. Past medical history is significant for ulcerative colitis diagnosed 2 years ago, well managed medically. He is vaccinated against hepatitis A and B and denies any recent travel abroad. On physical examination, prominent hepatosplenomegaly is noted. Which of the following would confirm the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
opb. Contrast CT of the abdomen
opc. Ultrasound of the abdomen
opd. Percutaneous liver biopsy
ope. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms of pruritus and jaundice, along with a history of ulcerative colitis and hepatosplenomegaly, suggest primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). Standard medical consensus indicates that MRCP is the non-invasive diagnostic test of choice for PSC, as it can visualize bile duct strictures characteristic of the disease. While ERCP can also show bile duct strictures, it is more invasive and typically used for therapeutic purposes rather than initial diagnosis. Liver biopsy can show onion-skin fibrosis, but it is not the primary diagnostic tool for PSC. Ultrasound and contrast CT can identify hepatosplenomegaly and possible bile duct abnormalities, respectively, but are not definitive for PSC diagnosis. Therefore, MRCP is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis of PSC in this patient.
